name: APY
seoDesc: APY: work out annual percentage rate of charge (APR) from the initial deposit and the annual percentage yield. A free finance calculator with the formula,…
summary: Give the APY calculator the initial deposit, the annual percentage yield and the term and it returns annual percentage rate of charge (APR). That makes it useful for a budget, a loan conversation, a payslip check or a what-if before you talk to a lender. The unit chips sit next to the boxes, which is where most hand-calculation mistakes start.

sections.title: How does the APY calculator work?
sections.html:
The APY calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports annual percentage rate of charge (APR) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the compound frequency); then you type in the initial deposit, the annual percentage yield (APY) and the term.

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• A measured quantity, entered by default in US Dollar. The unit chip switches it to any of the 113 supported units.
  • Pick the option that matches your case — 6 options, such as yearly, half-yearly and quarterly. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in percent. The unit chip switches it to any of the 6 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in months. The unit chip switches it to any of the 27 supported units.

1 field on this form is a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the APY calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Annual percentage rate of charge (APR)=compound frequency × ((annual percentage yield (APY) + 1 ^ 1 ÷ compound frequency) − 1)
Final deposit=initial deposit × ((compound frequency + annual percentage rate of charge (APR)) ÷ compound frequency, compound frequency × term)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Open the page and it is already filled in. With the values it starts from — Initial deposit = 10000, Annual percentage rate of charge (APR) = 5 %, Compound frequency set to Monthly and Term = 8766 mos — it reports Annual percentage yield (APY) = 5 %.

Those are real numbers produced by the same engine that runs when you press Calculate, so you can change any single box afterwards and watch the answer move from this starting point.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Annual percentage yield (APY) = 5 % should be roughly the size you expected from Initial deposit = 10000 and Annual percentage rate of charge (APR) = 5 %.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• Shown in percent, and convertible to any of the 6 units on that chip.
  • Shown in US Dollar, and convertible to any of the 113 units on that chip.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Currency, opening in US Dollar
  • %, opening in percent
  • %, opening in percent
  • Time, opening in months
  • Currency, opening in US Dollar

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The APY calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Preparing questions for a lender, an accountant or an adviser
  • Sizing up a purchase before you commit to it
  • Building a monthly budget and testing how one number shifts the rest
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the initial deposit, the annual percentage yield and the term — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the APY calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns annual percentage rate of charge (APR), derived from the initial deposit, the annual percentage yield and the term. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the APY calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the initial deposit, the annual percentage yield and the term, which is 4 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter initial deposit in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Initial deposit opens in US Dollar and the chip beside it offers 113 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Annual percentage yield (APY) = 5 %. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the APY calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
